Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Russia Moscow restaurant bombing kills three people as device carried by woman explodes More than 20 people injured in explosion near Italian restaurant on Saturday night, authorities say Reuters in Moscow Sat 1 Aug 2026 20.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A homemade bomb carried by a woman killed three people and injured at least 21 in ⁠an explosion near a restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, authorities said. The explosion occurred just before 8pm close to an Italian restaurant located in one of Moscow’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers at Kudrinskaya ​Square, the police said. Russia’s anti-terrorism ‌committee said an ‌unidentified woman had tried to get into the restaurant but was stopped by a security ‌guard, the state RIA news agency reported. It said the woman, the security guard and a customer at the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant were killed in the blast that followed. View image in fullscreen Officers stand guard at the Balzi Rossi restaurant. Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters Those injured received wounds of varying seriousness, the police said. Russia’s state RIA news agency released video of heavily armed law enforcement officers ‌at the scene, which had been closed off to the public. The authorities did not name those killed or injured nor did they ​say who they thought might have been responsible. View image in fullscreen The scene in central Moscow after the blast. Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters The Kommersant daily newspaper cited its own ​sources as saying that the ​bomb had been intended to ​maim and kill guests on the restaurant’s ​summer terrace outside. It suggested ‌the ​bomb had been ​set off by someone else remotely and that the woman carrying it may not have known it was a bomb. The restaurant’s website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event. https://lasvegassun.com/news/2026/jul/19.text: What to know about the Tate brothers, social media influencers facing rape and trafficking charges Published Sunday, July 19, 2026 | 4:48 a.m. Updated Monday, July 20, 2026 | 1:07 p.m. LONDON (AP) — Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate appeared before a federal magistrate Monday in Miami for the first time since prosecutors in the United Kingdom brought new rape and sex trafficking charges against them. Their lawyer said the brothers will fight extradition to the U.K. and suggested their arrest in Miami was politically motivated without explaining why. A U.S. district judge will consider in the weeks ahead whether they meet the conditions for extradition. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for July 27. The brothers have denied wrongdoing. Here are some things to know about the Tate brothers: Who the Tate Brothers are Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, are dual U.S.-British citizens known for their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny. Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X. He has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines. He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women. Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer. The brothers are avid supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump. What the Tates are charged with Andrew Tate and his brother have faced multiple charges in the U.K. and Romania , where they lived from 2016 to 2025. British prosecutors said the new charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2010 and 2017. They said Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault and 19 charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking. The Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement it “has requested the extradition of the Tates from the U.S. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the U.K.” The Tates already face previous charges of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. In June, a U.K. High Court judge threw out a legal bid by the Tates to be told the names of their accusers. In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women. The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. The case hasn’t been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania. Andrew Tate has repeatedly claimed that prosecutors in Romania have no evidence against him and that there is a political conspiracy to silence him. How the extradition process could work The brothers appeared Monday before a magistrate judge in Miami, where they were being held in federal detention. Bail is rarely granted to those held for international extradition, and their lawyer said he expects they will remain jailed for the time being. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. The ultimate decision about whether to order the extradition will fall to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While the State Department has some discretion to deny extradition requests from the U.K., it has granted nearly every British request since ratifying a strengthened extradition treaty in 2007. One exception came during Trump’s first term, when the U.S. declined an extradition request for the wife of a former American diplomat involved in a fatal crash in England , citing diplomatic immunity. The rejection prompted an international outcry. Why the Tates were in the U.S. British police previously sought the Tates' extradition to the U.K. once their legal proceedings in Romania concluded. But in February 2025 they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet. Romania's foreign minister said at the time that a U.S. official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers’ legal case in Romania. Trump said he knew “nothing about” the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romania government to release the Tates. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Police officers on the promenade at Catalans beach after the prefecture announced security measures for Marseille's beaches on 8 June 2026. Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images Opinion France From maligned second city to Insta magnet: Marseille is France’s new capital of overtourism Mary Fitzgerald This summer has been a tipping point. But it’s not too late to save what makes this place unique Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.15 EDT Share W hen I first started visiting Marseille more than 20 years ago, few could have predicted that France’s then beleaguered second city would become one of the most popular destinations in the most-visited country in the world . Tarnished by stereotypes and home to some of Europe’s most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, the port city seemed down on its luck, unloved and, in the eyes of many, somewhere to avoid. Tourists stopping at the city’s Saint-Charles station would clutch their bags while waiting for their connecting train to rural Provence, or the beaches of the Côte d’Azur. Two decades on, poverty and drug gang violence still affect parts of Marseille, but this rough diamond has been reinvented as a modish holiday destination. Last month, I saw a local TV channel asking whether Marseille had become France’s capital of tourism , after Booking.com revealed it had surpassed Paris and Nice as the most searched-for destination for French users of the site. Breathless foreign media coverage – the New York Times published a “36 hours in Marseille” guide in 2019 and another one in 2025 – has driven the number of overseas visitors. From seaside petanque to vocoder rap and pizza served on aluminium plates, influencers revel in the golden-hued aesthetic of the urban riviera and promote the city’s most Instagram-friendly corners. Tourist numbers are expected to reach almost 7 million this year . This has proved a boon for Marseille in many ways: more than 20,000 jobs are linked to the local tourism sector, which generates €1.4bn (£1.2bn) annually . But it has also prompted a heated debate over the challenges of overtourism. This summer has felt like something of a tipping point. In June, the inhabitants of Les Goudes, a rugged fishing hamlet on the city’s periphery that has become an Instagram magnet, took to the streets in protest . One resident said they were so overwhelmed by visitor numbers that they felt as if they were under house arrest. In Vallons des Auffes, another picturesque tourist favourite, local people are opposing a planned sixth restaurant in its tiny harbour. When swimming was banned at the heaving Plage des Catalans earlier this month due to bacterial contamination, many local people blamed overcrowding. Residents of other heavily frequented neighbourhoods are organising against what they see as dramatic touristification that has brought with it unprecedented levels of noise and litter, along with higher prices. Anti-Airbnb sentiment, often expressed in graffiti, has been building for several years; the platform began flourishing here partly due to a shortage of hotel rooms. Meanwhile, campaigns against cruise ships have gained popular support, even if local politicians are divided on the issue. View image in fullscreen MS Allure of the Seas, the largest passenger ship ever constructed, leaving the port of Marseille. Photograph: Boris Horvat/AFP/Getty Images It’s common to hear Marseillais say they don’t want their city to become another Barcelona or Lisbon; the problem here has been the breakneck speed of the transformation. When I made the city my home almost a decade ago, tourism remained relatively low key. Local newspaper La Provence recently noted that it was in summer 2020 – when masses of French visitors descended on Marseille after months of pandemic lockdown – that the city first discovered overtourism. As is usually the case, the subsequent deluge of tourists is accompanied by a wave of gentrification that has driven up property prices and stirred local resentment. It feels like we blinked, and suddenly a Marseille summer meant thronged beaches, sprawling mega-bars, long queues for public transport and streets full of tour groups, mobile disco buses and – the most obnoxious canary in the coalmine – neon-lit pedicabs blaring loud music. Friends who grew up here and now have families of their own lament that typical child-friendly summer activities now involve advance bookings and snaking queues. As most local people agree, the problem is not tourism per se – the jobs it creates help dent the city’s high unemployment – but this record-breaking surge needs to be better managed and regulated. Local authorities insist that they are prioritising sustainability. The city hall, which has been ruled by a Green-left alliance since 2020, includes a deputy mayor with responsibility for sustainable tourism . When the new president of Marseille’s tourism office was appointed in June, he said he wanted to ensure that tourism primarily benefits Marseille’s citizens . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Fight them for the beaches: the real villain of Europe’s overtourism is big business | Adam Almeida Read more Some concrete measures have been introduced in recent years. In 2024, our mayor, Benoît Payan, brought in France’s toughest restrictions on Airbnb (even if implementation has been a challenge). Daily visitor quotas have been imposed on parts of the Calanques, a maritime park within the city limits that is popular with hikers and day trippers, to protect its fragile ecosystem. There are efforts to encourage more off-season visitors, and to diversify the predictable Instagram (and PR)-led tourist trail that results in overcrowding. But the political battle over whether the city should expand or limit cruise-ship infrastructure continues. City hall’s critics argue that the overtourism challenge is being met with a patchwork of interventions rather than a muscular overall policy. Some residents want to see higher tourist taxes or dual pricing, whereby visitors pay more for public transport and other amenities. Others seek even stricter limits on Airbnb. There are also demands that the most inundated districts, such as Les Goudes, are closed to visitors’ cars. At the very least, more substantive public awareness campaigns asking tourists not to litter or cause disturbances in residential neighbourhoods would help. What all of us share is the worry that time is running out, and Marseille will become yet another European city that seems to cater more for visitors than its own inhabitants. It’s a delicate balance to strike, but Marseille is still at the stage where it can learn from the cautionary tales elsewhere, mitigate the worst excesses and strive to preserve what made the city worth visiting in the first place. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw.text: Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos By Monica Garnsey BBC Eye Published 2 hours ago Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia. One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil. He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs. The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves. He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities. The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself." And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out. The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this. There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify. Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia. Watch on iPlayer Listen to the Podcast on BBC Sounds. If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube , external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome. "At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says. His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets. "When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said. He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield. If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades. Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance. Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers "You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers. Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information. He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets. "This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live. "In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points." He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints. Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals. "As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not." But he argued that his team's actions were justified. "I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared." Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves. Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule." But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance. Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event. Foma did his own digging on Ivan. After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year , external . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians. Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too. "The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said. To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside. Foma has the same rule for his operatives. "As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said. Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work. "Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said. Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands. Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities. So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return. Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him. "You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him. Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school". But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress. Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag. "There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon. Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where. Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work. "Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia." But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change. "Putin won't live forever," he said.
